Need to search first.Fewer at once.I've written notes on all 22 verses, but sections 2 and 3 are thin. My research tools hit their usage limit early, so I could open only a handful of pages directly. Most of what follows comes from the text the search tool returned, which for some pages was cut off.

**What's missing as a result:**
- **Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran views:** I found nothing on newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, lcms.org or 1517.org. Precept Austin's resource page lists Kretzmann's Lutheran commentary, but I didn't read it.
- **NET Bible notes:** none.
- **Prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching:** nothing on this chapter.
- **Section 2 (Protestant traditions):** I found no clear split along denominational lines. The real disagreements I found are between individual commentators, mainly on vv. 2 and 7.

The pages describe only Wesley's tradition (StudyLight tags him "Arminian, Wesleyan/Methodist"). Any other denominational labels below are my own.

---

## Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- Benson says Moses repeats the three yearly feasts to guard against idolatry: they kept the people loyal to the one true God at the national place of worship. He takes "by night" to mean Pharaoh gave permission that night, with the departure completed in the morning. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/16-1.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) explains Abib as the month of ripening barley, roughly late March to early April. It admits "by night" seems to clash with Exodus 12:22 and Numbers 33:3, which place the departure in the morning, but says the two can be reconciled. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/deuteronomy/16.htm
- Precept Austin notes that "observe" occurs about 73 times in Deuteronomy and echoes the Sabbath command (5:12). Curry, quoted there, says the whole festival calendar in this chapter is patterned on the weekly Sabbath. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-16-commentary
- Enduring Word (Guzik) sees Passover as a picture of Jesus the Passover Lamb (1 Cor 5:7), whose applied blood turns God's wrath away from believers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-16/

**v. 2: "from the herd or flock" (commentators disagree)**
- Exodus 12 allows only a lamb. Currid, quoted on Precept Austin, flags this as an apparent conflict. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-16-commentary
- Guzik gives three options: God accepted other animals; the cattle belonged to the Unleavened Bread sacrifices; or they were extra sacrifices. He cites the Passovers of Josiah and Hezekiah (2 Chr 35:7; 30:24). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-16/
- Gill says the Passover proper was only a lamb, and the cattle refer to the offerings of the seven days (Num 28:19). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-16.html Keil & Delitzsch agree, adding that an ox never replaced the lamb. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/16-3.htm J. Orr (Pulpit Homiletics) takes the same view. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/deuteronomy/16.htm
- On "the place": Guzik notes the shift from home sacrifice in Egypt to the tabernacle, later the temple. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-16/ Benson says sacrifice was valid only at the altar. Keeping people at the chosen place also kept them to the rules, away from their own inventions, and pointed to where the Messiah, the true Passover, would die. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/benson/deuteronomy/16.htm

**v. 3: "bread of affliction"**
- **Clarke:** the bread was unpleasant to eat and so reminded them of their bondage. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/deuteronomy/16.htm
- **Gill:** either the bread was heavy and hard to digest, or (his preference, following Jarchi) it was meant to recall the affliction in Egypt. He notes the Jewish custom of breaking matzah and calling it "the bread of affliction." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-16.html
- **Pulpit Commentary:** bread made in a time of pressure, with no chance to make better bread. **Geneva Bible note:** it signified their affliction in Egypt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/16-3.htm
- **Calvin:** they fled "as it were from the very flames," and remembering it magnifies God's grace. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom03.vi.iii.v.html
- **Matthew Henry:** the memory was meant to last "all the days of thy life" and to keep moving them to obey. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_016.cfm
- **Utley (Bible.org):** joined to Passover, the feast kept God's gracious deliverance always in view. https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-16

**v. 4**
- Guzik: leaven pictures sin, because a little spreads through the whole lump and it "puffs up" the dough the way pride does. Unleavened Bread pictures pure living after blood deliverance, and prophetically Jesus' burial. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-16/
- Orr links this to 1 Cor 5:8: the feast stands for the holy life that follows salvation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/deuteronomy/16.htm
- Clarke: the meat had to be eaten fresh because it spoiled quickly in that climate. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/deuteronomy/16.htm
- Gill: every room and crevice was searched for leaven beforehand. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-16.html

**v. 5**
- Precept Austin: Moses is mainly speaking to the children of the exodus generation, and each generation should picture itself in that first one's place. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-16-commentary
- Matthew Henry, quoted on StudyLight: the Passover could be sacrificed at the chosen place and nowhere else. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/16-6.html
- Bible Hub's Q&A page sees no contradiction with Exodus 12. Egypt had no sanctuary, and the central site guarded against idolatry and united the nation. https://biblehub.com/q/how_to_reconcile_passover_sacrifice_sites.htm

**v. 6**
- **Gill:** the place where the ark and the Shekinah dwelt, which was Jerusalem. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/16-6.html
- **Coffman:** only one Passover was kept in the wilderness (Num 9), so the instruction prepares for life in the land. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/16-7.html
- **On "twilight":** Precept Austin's note prefers 3–5 p.m., which allows time for many sacrifices at the sanctuary. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-16-commentary JFB argues the priests could manage the huge number of victims within a few hours. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/deuteronomy/16.htm
- **Keil & Delitzsch on Ellicott's page:** the date recalled is the slaying of the lamb on the 14th rather than the march itself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/16-1.htm

**v. 7: "return to your tents" (a real difference)**
- **Wesley (Methodist):** the morning after the seventh day. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/16-7.html
- **Gill and Benson:** also after the seven days, since the first day was a holy assembly. Benson calls the words a permission, not a command. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-16.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/benson/deuteronomy/16.htm
- **JFB:** at first sight it means the next morning, but leans toward after the seven days. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/deuteronomy/16.htm
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** the next morning, back to lodgings at the sanctuary town, not home. Moses still requires the seven days (v. 8). They add that roasting and eating at the sanctuary quietly ended the custom of smearing blood on doorposts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/16-1.htm
- **Cambridge Bible (critical):** finds a one-day feast in v. 7 hard to square with the seven days, and sees separate sources. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/16-1.htm

**v. 8**
- Gill: unleavened bread was still eaten on day seven. That day is singled out only for its special service. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-16.html
- The Cambridge Bible notes that the count works if the Passover day is included, but finds it odd that it isn't mentioned. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/deuteronomy/16.htm

**v. 9**
- Cambridge Bible: the starting point (first sickle) varied, unlike the fixed date in Lev 23:15. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/deuteronomy/16.htm
- Wiersbe (on Precept Austin) reads Pentecost as renewal and the coming of the Spirit (Acts 2), and a call to help reap the harvest. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-16-commentary

**v. 10**
- Guzik: the offering was proportional, so those blessed more gave more. There was no required animal sacrifice, only joyful thanks. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-16/
- Precept Austin: a freewill offering comes from devotion, not compulsion. It also reads Acts 2 as fulfilment: no atoning sacrifice was needed because Jesus had already paid. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-16-commentary
- Benson: this was a voluntary gift on top of the sacrifices required in Num 28 and Lev 23. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/benson/deuteronomy/16.htm

**v. 11**
- Clarke: the offerings were to be shared generously with friends and the poor. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/deuteronomy/16.htm
- Guzik: every feast made room for the vulnerable. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-16/
- Cambridge Bible: including women (daughters, maidservants, widows) is typical of Deuteronomy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/deuteronomy/16.htm

**v. 12**
- Matthew Henry: the Feast of Weeks recalled the law given at Sinai fifty days after the exodus, so the best thanks is to obey it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_016.cfm
- Gill: their redemption from slavery should make them generous, just as redemption by Christ moves believers to good works. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/16.htm
- Precept Austin, quoting Utley and a devotional: having been slaves, Israel could show tenderness to the stranger and the widow. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-16-commentary

**v. 13**
- Guzik dates the feast to the 15th of Tishri. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-16/
- JFB notes various guesses about why it falls at the end of harvest. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/deuteronomy/16.htm

**v. 14**
- The Cambridge Bible mentions Steuernagel's suggestion that the repeated command to rejoice shows the feast had lost its joy. It thinks this doesn't prove the point. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/deuteronomy/16.htm

**v. 15**
- Precept Austin: "surely" or "complete" is emphatic in Hebrew, and Deuteronomy stresses rejoicing at the feasts more than any other book of the Pentateuch. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-16-commentary
- **Wiersbe:** Tabernacles reminds Christians they are pilgrims, and it points ahead to the coming kingdom. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-16-commentary
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** sees the feast pointing to the Millennium (Zech 14:16–19). That is a specifically premillennial reading. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-16/
- **Pulpit Homiletics:** the rest is found in Christ now but fully only in eternity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/deuteronomy/16.htm

**v. 16**
- **Why only men:** JFB and Poole say women were spared the long journeys because of physical strain and family duties. Poole adds that the men represented them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/16-16.htm
- **Gill:** the verse is repeated from Exodus 23 mainly to specify the place. He cites New Testament pilgrimages (Luke 2:42; Acts 2:5; John 7:2). Same URL.
- **Unity:** Matthew Henry and Benson say meeting often in one place kept Israel faithful and united. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_016.cfm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/benson/deuteronomy/16.htm
- **Precept Austin:** Moses picks three of the seven feasts. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-16-commentary

**v. 17**
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** "not empty-handed" means sacrificial gifts in proportion to God's blessing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/16-16.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** the offering showed dependence on God and gratitude. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_016.cfm
- **Precept Austin:** treats this as a good rule for Christian giving generally. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-16-commentary

**v. 18**
- **Clarke:** compares judges to magistrates, and officers to men who checked weights and measures. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/deuteronomy/16.htm
- **JFB:** the city gate was where cases were decided. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/16-18.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** the shoterim were clerks and assessors to the judges. Same URL.
- **Unnamed note on that page:** larger towns later had courts of 23 judges, smaller ones courts of three. Same URL.
- **Constable:** places 16:18 to 18:22 under the fifth commandment, about respecting authority. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-16.html

**v. 19**
- Benson: judges must not rule by a person's wealth, friendship or enmity. A bribe bends even the mind of an honest judge. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/benson/deuteronomy/16.htm
- Precept Austin: "show partiality" literally means "recognise faces." It lists biblical examples of bribery, from Delilah to Felix. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-16-commentary

**v. 20: "justice, justice"**
- The Pulpit Commentary says the doubling adds emphasis. The Cambridge Bible says it means to hunt after justice tirelessly. Gill reads it as strict justice and nothing else. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/16-20.htm
- Deere, quoted on Precept Austin, says the wording admits impartial justice is hard for weak humans to reach. Precept Austin adds that Israel's stay in the land depended on obedience. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-16-commentary
- A critical note on Bible Hub's v. 18 page suggests the end of v. 20 may be a later scribe's addition. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/16-18.htm

**v. 21: Asherah**
- **Barnes:** an image of Astarte. **Pulpit Commentary:** a wooden pillar-idol set beside Baal's altars. **Keil & Delitzsch:** the word can't mean a grove. **Gill:** planting trees was fine, but not for worship. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/16-21.htm
- **Benson:** planting groves to honour God was an early custom (Gen 21:33), but they came to tempt people to idolatry. Same URL.
- **Clarke:** groves around idol temples hid obscene rites, and God's worship was to be done in public. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/deuteronomy/16.htm
- **Constable:** Asherah was both a Canaanite goddess and an object used to worship her. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-16.html

**v. 22**
- Matthew Henry: nothing misrepresents God, who is spirit, more than worshipping him through an image. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_016.cfm
- Constable: sacred pillars were used for both Baal and Asherah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-16.html
- The Cambridge Bible notes that Hosea seems to treat pillars as normal at the LORD's shrines in northern Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/deuteronomy/16.htm

---

## Other views: modern scholarship (vv. 2, 5–6, 16)

- **Bible Odyssey:** before King Josiah centralised worship in the 7th century BC, feasts were held locally or at home. His reform united worship in Jerusalem based on a rediscovered "book of the law." https://bibleodyssey.org/passages/main-articles/festivals-in-the-hebrew-bible-deuteronomy-16
- **Cambridge Bible (critical):** Deuteronomy moved all three feasts from rural shrines to one altar. It also sees signs that Passover and Unleavened Bread were once separate feasts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/deuteronomy/16.htm
- **Evangelical reply (Themelios, on The Gospel Coalition site):** "the place the LORD will choose" is the main argument for a 7th-century date. But Deuteronomy never names Jerusalem, and 2 Kings 22–23 doesn't clearly show the reforms came from the discovered book.
  - https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/the-date-of-deuteronomy-linch-pin-of-old-testament-criticism/
  - https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/the-date-of-deuteronomy-linch-pin-of-old-testament-criticism-part-2/
